rationale: The construct is internally consistent and correctly signed, but netting Δcapx against Δcash and swapping a 3-year profitability trend for a one-period delta is largely a re-parameterization of the archive's best signal (Liquidity-Depleting Post-Peak Expansion) rather than a new mechanism, and the subtraction also allows a large cash build to be offset by a large capex cut, blurring the intended "resource pressure" interpretation.

This is a single-operator mutation (NEG→ABS) of the archive's Undermaintenance Profit Erosion, and because ABS pools two economically opposite groups—overinvestors and undermaintainers—any negative slope will most likely be inherited from the already-documented undermaintenance tail in diluted form, while the positive-sign evidence from Maintenance-Balanced Cash Generator makes the pooled hypothesis hard to interpret either way.

A three-year sum of capex/at is essentially the well-known capital-investment/asset-growth anomaly in level form, and pairing it with a declining profitability trend reproduces the structure of the archive's Post-Peak Capex Commitment and Peak-Profit Capex Lag (both weak), so this offers little incremental information.

Substituting firm-specific distance from a log-sales peak for the previously tested profitability-peak distance introduces genuinely different information (demand recession rather than margin erosion), the expression matches the stated hypothesis and sign, and the denominator-free demand measure sensibly avoids the capex-inflated-asset confound.

The cash-conversion leg is mechanically contaminated because oiadp is after depreciation while oancf adds it back, so capex-heavy firms with rising D&A tend to have a *falling* oiadp−oancf gap—working against the very conjunction the MIN requires—and the archive's oibdp-based Goodwill Cash Conversion Break already tested the cleaner version with negligible alpha.

The hypothesis is economically sensible, but the triple MIN over falling cash, falling operating income, and falling capex will be dominated by the deteriorating-fundamentals legs—effectively a distress/profitability-decline signal already spanned by known anomalies—and the fact that the exact opposite capex direction "worked" in the archive winner suggests the capex leg carries little independent information at very thin coverage.
